analysis.one_liner: Caps medical malpractice damages and lawyer fees and shields FDA-approved drug and device makers from punitive damages.
analysis.headline: Introduced in March 1995 with three Republican cosponsors, the bill was sent to the House Judiciary Committee and never received a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rewritten the rules for every medical malpractice case in the country. It required injured patients to first go through a government-certified alternative dispute system before suing, capped pain-and-suffering damages at $250,000, shortened the deadline to sue to one year from discovery of the injury, cut the percentage lawyers could charge, and reduced any award by amounts the patient already received from insurance or disability programs. It also barred punitive damages against drug and device makers whose products were approved by the FDA. The federal rules would have overridden any state law that gave patients more time or more compensation.
analysis.who_benefits: Health care providers, hospitals, medical malpractice insurers, and drug and device manufacturers. Providers would face lower malpractice insurance premiums and less exposure to large jury awards; insurers would pay out less; manufacturers of FDA-approved products would be immune from punitive damages except in cases of fraud on the FDA or bribery of an official [S3]. Supporters also argued patients would benefit from lower health care costs and faster resolution of claims through the mandatory alternative dispute systems [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Doctors, hospitals, malpractice insurers, drug makers

how_it_helps.text: Caps total noneconomic (pain-and-suffering) damages at $250,000 per injury no matter how many defendants or lawsuits are involved [S3].
Caps contingency fees on a sliding scale: 25% of the first $100,000 recovered, down to 10% of anything over $500,000, leaving patients a larger share of any award [S3].
Bars punitive damages against manufacturers or distributors of FDA-approved medical products unless they knowingly misled the FDA or bribed an official to win approval [S3].

Requires every malpractice claim to first be resolved through an alternative dispute resolution system, with a written decision within six months, and penalizes any party who contests the ruling in court and does not improve their position by at least 10% by paying the other side's attorney fees and costs [S3].
The bill's findings assert that malpractice litigation contributes to high health care costs and malpractice insurance premiums, which the reforms were meant to reduce [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Patients seriously injured by medical negligence. A $250,000 cap on pain-and-suffering damages applies even to catastrophic injuries like a child injured for life, and it is the only cap regardless of the number of defendants. Awards would be reduced dollar-for-dollar by insurance or disability payments, lawsuits would have to be filed within one year of discovering the injury, and each defendant would pay only its own share of fault even if other responsible parties cannot be found or are insolvent [S3]. State laws that give patients longer to sue or greater recovery would be overridden [S3].

drawbacks.text: The $250,000 cap on noneconomic damages applies to every injury combined, including cases of severe disfigurement, brain damage, or a child's wrongful death, and is not adjusted for inflation [S3].
The one-year statute of limitations from discovery, with an absolute three-year limit, is shorter than the deadlines many states allow and would bar some claims patients would otherwise have [S3].

Replacing jury trials with mandatory alternative dispute resolution, plus fee-shifting and a performance bond requirement for parties who contest the ADR decision without improving their position by 10%, could deter patients with valid claims from going to court [S3].

Dropping joint liability means an injured patient collects only each defendant's proportionate share, so if a largely responsible party is insolvent or unidentified, the patient absorbs the shortfall [S3].

Allowing state professional societies to participate in licensing and review malpractice claims, with confidentiality requirements and immunity for reviewers, gives physician trade associations a role in policing their own members [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill delivers a clear, one-directional benefit to providers, insurers, and manufacturers: lower liability exposure and lower premiums, which supporters said would lower health care costs. The cost falls on the relatively small number of patients with the most serious injuries, who would face a hard cap on the part of their compensation that covers pain and lost enjoyment of life, shorter filing deadlines, reduced awards from collateral-source offsets, and a mandatory non-jury process. The fee caps do leave winning patients a larger share of smaller awards, but a patient with a catastrophic injury would almost certainly receive far less than under state law. On balance the bill's gains flow to industry while its costs are borne by injured patients.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on March 9, 1995, sent to the House Judiciary Committee, and sat there without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote until the Congress ended in January 1997 [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Bob Stump introduced the Health Care Liability Reform Act of 1995 on March 9, 1995, joined by Reps. Callahan and Everett [S3].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day [S5].
It had three cosponsors, all Republicans [S4].
No further action was taken; the bill never left committee and died when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Injured patients keep whatever remedies their state law provides today, with no federal cap on damages or shortened deadlines. Providers, malpractice insurers, and drug and device makers do not get the federal liability limits they sought. The committee's inaction preserved the status quo for both sides.

for.name: Reps. Sonny Callahan and Terry Everett
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill's introduction on March 9, 1995

against.name: House Committee on the Judiciary
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on March 9, 1995 and never scheduled a hearing or markup, leaving the bill to die at the end of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced and cosponsored exclusively by Republicans (three cosponsors in total), and no hearings, votes, or Democratic involvement appear in the record; there was never a roll call to measure bipartisan support [S4][S5].

industries.note: Damage caps, mandatory ADR, fee limits, and collateral-source offsets all reduce what insurers must pay on claims. Their gain comes directly out of the compensation available to injured patients.

industries.industry: Physicians, hospitals, and other health care providers
industries.note: The bill caps their malpractice exposure and lowers the premiums they pay, and lets professional societies participate in licensing and malpractice review with confidentiality and immunity. Patients' ability to hold them fully accountable in court would shrink.

Manufacturers of FDA-approved products would be immune from punitive damages except where they defrauded the FDA or bribed an official, sharply limiting the strongest financial deterrent against unsafe products.

Contingency fees would be capped on a sliding scale and mandatory ADR plus fee-shifting would cut into the volume and economics of malpractice litigation. Their business is closely tied to patients' access to compensation.
